results.title: Integration of Model-Based Systems Engineering and Life Cycle Assessment to Consider Environmental Impacts During Conceptual Design
results.abstract: Technical products generate environmental impacts throughout their life cycle, particularly during production, use, and end-of-life. Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) is a well-established method for quantifying these impacts; however, it typically emphasizes the production or use phase and insufficiently accounts for varying use scenarios or system configurations. This limitation reduces its effectiveness in supporting product design decisions. The objective of this publication is to enable LCA as a prospective method in early design stages. Achieving this requires consideration of both technical product properties and application scenarios, as these factors strongly influence life cycle impacts. To address this, we propose a concept for integrating Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) with LCA. The approach combines use case analysis to identify application scenarios with SysML block elements representing product objects. These blocks carry product properties, application-specific data, and environmental information, which are provided to the LCA to estimate expected impacts during conceptual design. The calculated results are then reintegrated into the SysML model, linking environmental performance directly to system architecture. results.title: APPLICATION OF MODEL-BASED SYSTEMS ENGINEERING METHODS TO ADVANCED ENERGY LOCOMOTIVE DESIGN AND OPTIMIZATION
results.abstract: Diesel-electric locomotives are highly complex systems integrating complex subsystems across multiple domains, making their design and development time consuming. As the rail industry transitions toward advanced energy locomotive technologies, reducing development time and enhancing design efficiency are critical. Model-Based Design (MBD) offers a streamlined approach by leveraging mathematical models to simulate, analyze, and validate system behavior prior to physical prototyping. This paper introduces Autonomie Rail, a novel rail simulation tool developed to support the evaluation and optimization of alternative energy locomotives in a well-organized way using modern software techniques. Autonomie Rail speeds up the model development and simulation process by allowing users to create, manage, share and reuse physical component models and automating vehicle model building processes. Autonomie Rail extends Argonne National Laboratory's Autonomie framework, originally designed for automotive applications [1]. It provides a flexible, modular simulation environment using MATLAB, Simulink, and Stateflow for dynamic modeling, coupled with a C# based graphical user interface for enhanced user interaction. The tool enables engineers to perform comprehensive system-level simulations, optimize energy management strategies, and refine control algorithms efficiently. This paper provides an overview of Autonomie Rail and discusses its application through mainline freight rail case studies on battery-electric and hydrogen fuel cell locomotives. While most of the points in this paper are examined from the perspective of freight locomotives, they can also be thoughtfully applied to commuter and passenger trains.

results.title: A Review on the Application of Model-Based Systems Engineering in the Development of Safe Circular Systems
results.abstract: The increasing complexity of modern technical systems, coupled with the growing demand for sustainability and safety, necessitates innovative approaches in system development. Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) has emerged as a powerful methodology to support the development process of such complex systems. This paper presents a systematic literature review that explores the role of MBSE in the development of sustainable and safe systems. The study classifies existing design supports by analyzing their role in the development process across three key areas: sustainability, safety risk, and knowledge management. The findings reveal current challenges, such as fragmented lifecycle data, limited automation in safety analysis, and difficulties in reusing expert knowledge, while also identifying research opportunities for AI-driven methods, digital twin utilization, and enhanced interoperability between MBSE and lifecycle management tools. By consolidating the class supported activities and their interactions, this paper provides insights into how MBSE can facilitate circularity in system development and highlights directions for future research.

results.title: Considerations for Implementation of Model-Based Systems Engineering in Different Sectors and System Types Based on Academic Literature
results.abstract: The emergence and adoption of Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) is driven in part by claimed benefits over traditional Document-Based Systems Engineering. Despite high enthusiasm for MBSE, few studies have evaluated the value of MBSE implementation or the needs in MBSE implementation across various system types and industry sectors, which may require differing drivers of implementation and analyses of added value. This study investigates the perceptions of MBSE across sectors including Commercial, Contractor, and Government, as well as across system types including Astronautical, Aeronautical, and Infrastructure, to determine the perceived drivers and considerations of MBSE implementation across different industries. From 60 academic sources, this study collected and coded over 2900 claims about MBSE using 68 MBSE attributes. Our study's findings determine that the considerations for MBSE implementation likely vary by both sector and by system. Perceptions of MBSE, regardless of application grouping, were largely positive-negative attributes often captured unfavorable perceptions of implementation and tooling immaturity. The findings of this study suggest that practitioners may need to tailor the implementation of MBSE partly to their organizational priorities and needs, and to be cautious of relying only on broadly reported benefits of MBSE.

results.title: Survey of model-based systems engineering (MBSE): State of practice, perception and aligning academic instructions with industry needs
results.abstract: To address the rising demand for MBSE use in industry, academia must first grasp the industry's view of MBSE. To facilitate this process, we share quantitative and qualitative data from a survey of the current state of practice and perception of MBSE in the UK landscape. Our study provides a discourse on academia's self-assessment of the extent to which academia can provide the graduating class with important MBSE abilities to tackle real-world problems. To this day, the most significant challenges to adoption include organisational opposition and structure, a shortage of qualified workers, and the availability of MBSE instruments. Respondents agreed that MBSE tasks such as behavioural modelling, verification, and validation should be included in the teaching curriculum. Based on these findings, we propose academic techniques for designing MBSE instruction within the aerospace engineering degree curriculum. Finally, we explore the obstacles and constraints that academia encounters in implementing MBSE in a curriculum, and some solutions are proposed.
